lessons.title: After a win
lessons.objective: You can respond warmly to a happy fan.

payload.title: She scored a worldie
payload.setting: She texts right after her team scores a spectacular goal.

exchanges.theirMessage: DID YOU SEE THAT?? From thirty yards, top corner, no chance!

replies.text: That was an absolute worldie. Where was she when she struck it?
replies.theirResponse: Just inside the box, saw the keeper off his line and just bent it.
replies.coachNote: Shows you spotted the beauty and asks about the setup.

replies.text: Nice shot!
replies.coachNote: Honest but missing the excitement she's sharing.

replies.text: Goals like that happen every game.
replies.coachNote: Never minimize what she loves.

payload.closingNote: She is celebrating a spectacular goal from range; match her energy while asking about the moment.

statement.speaker: Rashida
statement.text: Fourth clean sheet in a row, that back four is locked in.
statement.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: Her team has not conceded a goal in the last four matches
Her team's defence has committed four fouls
Four goals were scored in shut-out fashion
The back line has kept opponents from scoring

statement.translation: A clean sheet is a match with no goals conceded. Four in a row means the defence is playing at a high level.

followUps.line: How many clean sheets does your team usually get a season?
followUps.why: It opens a conversation about defensive consistency.

followUps.line: Is it the keeper or the back line keeping them tight?
followUps.why: Asks her to spot what's working without claiming expertise.

statement.noFakeExpertNote: If you don't know their recent form, ask 'Is that unusual for them?' or 'Who's been the standout defender?'

payload.prompt: A fan says a goal was a worldie. What does she mean?

options.text: It was the best goal of the World Cup

text.text: It was a spectacular goal from an improbable angle
She watches the world feed
All goals worldwide count

explanation.correct: Right. A worldie is a stunning goal, usually from range or a tight angle.
explanation.incorrect: A worldie is fan slang for a spectacular, memorable goal that leaves you speechless.
explanation.sayThisLine: That was a worldie if I've ever seen one.

payload.prompt: Match the win-related term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A match in which a team concedes no goals.
A spectacular, beautiful goal that feels almost unforgettable.
A victory where the opponent scores nothing.

explanation.summary: These celebrate excellence in different ways: the defence (clean sheet) and the attack (worldie).
explanation.sayThisLine: A worldie in a clean sheet win, that's the dream.

payload.prompt: After a clean sheet win, which response works best?

options.text: Your defence was flawless.

text.text: Your keeper had an easy game.
What a defensive performance; who stood out to you?
Finally, a proper win.

explanation.correct: Good choice. It acknowledges what you noticed and asks her to share what she saw.
explanation.incorrect: The best responses match her excitement and ask a genuine question, not assume who was best.
explanation.sayThisLine: What a performance at the back.

payload.title: After a loss
payload.objective: You can respond to disappointment without being flippant.

payload.title: She's upset after a collapse
payload.setting: She texts after her team squanders a lead late in the match.

exchanges.theirMessage: Two-nil up at half. TWO-NIL. And we lose 3-2. I can't even look at the table.

replies.text: That's a hard one. What happened in the second half?
replies.theirResponse: We went to sleep. They pressed and we just panicked.
replies.coachNote: Empathy, then curiosity about the tactical detail.

replies.text: At least you scored two.
replies.coachNote: True but dismissive when she's hurting.

replies.text: Your team's bottling it this season anyway.
replies.coachNote: Never pile on when she's down.

payload.closingNote: She's frustrated about wasting a commanding position; ask about the tactical shift, not the outcome.

statement.speaker: Jordan
statement.text: We were clinical. They were wasteful. We took our chances.
statement.question: What is he saying?

options.text: His team finished their chances; the opponent missed theirs
Both teams played a medical style
His team was efficient in front of goal while the opponent wasted opportunities
The referee made clinical decisions

statement.translation: Clinical means taking chances efficiently; wasteful means creating chances but missing them. He's saying his team was ruthless and the opponent was poor at finishing.

followUps.line: How many big chances did each side have?
followUps.why: It tests whether both teams really had the same quality of opportunity.

followUps.line: Does your team usually finish this well?
followUps.why: Asks if this is a pattern or just this match.

statement.noFakeExpertNote: If the scoreline doesn't match the chances, ask to see the xG stat; it tells a deeper story than just the final result.

payload.prompt: A fan says 'We bottled it.' What happened?

options.text: The team threw away a winning position under pressure

text.text: The goalkeeper made an error
The team was leading and collapsed at the end
A player physically lost his grip on the ball

explanation.correct: Yes. Bottling is losing your nerve in a big moment when you had it in control.
explanation.incorrect: Bottling means collapsing under pressure when you had a winning position; it's about mentality, not individual errors.
explanation.sayThisLine: They bottled it in the final ten minutes.

payload.prompt: After a loss where your team bottled it, your friend looks angry. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what went wrong in the second half
Tell her the ref cost you the match
Point out the score doesn't really matter
Give her space and text later asking how she's doing

explanation.best: Good call. She wants to talk about what happened, and this shows you're listening.
explanation.acceptable: Right idea to respect her mood, but asking now shows you care.
explanation.poor: Don't blame the ref to a distraught fan, and don't minimize the loss.

payload.coachNote: After a loss, empathy comes first. Asking how the team threw it away is curiosity, not dismissal.

payload.prompt: Your friend says 'We were wasteful today.' What does this mean?

options.text: The team made poor passes

text.text: The team created chances but didn't finish them efficiently
The goalkeeper wasted time
The team wasted energy on running

explanation.correct: Right. Wasteful means having opportunities but failing to convert them.
explanation.incorrect: Wasteful in football means missing chances or poor finishing despite having the ball in good positions.
explanation.sayThisLine: We had the chances but we were wasteful in front of goal.

payload.title: Talking about the referee
payload.objective: You can join a referee complaint without picking a fight.

payload.title: Handball debate
payload.setting: She texts during a match where the ref refused to give a handball penalty.

exchanges.theirMessage: His arm was OUT. How is that not a handball?? Awful ref.

replies.text: Was his arm unnaturally big or deliberately up, or was it by his side?
replies.theirResponse: Actually now you say it, his arm was... sort of naturally positioned. Maybe not a pen.
replies.coachNote: Asking the right question helps her think it through without dismissing her anger.

replies.text: Yeah, that ref is terrible.
replies.coachNote: Agreement feels good but doesn't deepen the conversation.

replies.text: You don't know the handball rule.
replies.coachNote: Never talk down to a fan, even if she's frustrated.

payload.closingNote: She's angry about a decision; asking whether it was deliberate or unnatural helps her see the grey areas in handball.

statement.speaker: Alex
statement.text: He was offside but he never touched it, so no offence.
statement.question: What is Alex saying?

options.text: A player can stand in an offside position without committing an offence if not involved in play
If a player is offside they will always be penalised
Offside only applies if a player deliberately touches the ball
The goalkeeper made the decision to not blow the whistle

statement.translation: Being in an offside position is not itself an offence; it's only an offence if you interfere with play or gain an advantage from the position.

followUps.line: Did the player interfere with the keeper's view?
followUps.why: This tests whether passive standing in an offside position matters.

followUps.line: Who usually decides if a player is interfering?
followUps.why: Encourages understanding of the referee's judgment.

statement.noFakeExpertNote: The 'offside position' vs 'offside offence' distinction confuses many fans; it's okay to say 'I need to see a replay to judge if he was involved.'

payload.prompt: Defender's arm is glued to his body, ball hits it from close range. Handball?

scene.alt: A defender in the box with arms tight to his sides. A cross hits his shoulder/upper arm from very close range.

explanation.correct: Right. An arm in a natural position does not make the body unnaturally bigger, so it's usually not an offence.
explanation.incorrect: Handball is about deliberate contact or making your body bigger. A tight arm is a natural shape.
explanation.sayThisLine: His arm was in a natural position, that's why it wasn't a penalty.

payload.prompt: Match the referee concept to its definition.

pairs.definition: Deliberately touching the ball with hand or arm, or making the body unnaturally bigger.
Standing nearer to the goal than the second-last opponent at the moment of the pass.
Gaining an advantage or interfering in play while in an offside position.

explanation.summary: Position is not the same as the offence; similarly, a handball is about the body, not just the arm.
explanation.sayThisLine: There's a difference between being in an offside position and committing an offence.

payload.prompt: When should you acknowledge a referee call even if you disagree?

options.text: Never, if it cost your team

text.text: After the match, when emotions are cooler
Only if your team is winning
Immediately, to show good sportsmanship

explanation.correct: Good call. The referee's decision stands; talking it through later is fairer to everyone.
explanation.incorrect: It's natural to be angry, but the best conversations about decisions happen after emotions cool, not during the match.
explanation.sayThisLine: Let's talk about that call after the final whistle.

payload.title: Talking tactics
payload.objective: You can ask a good tactical question.

payload.title: She explains the tactical battle
payload.setting: She texts during a match where her team changed defensive shape.

exchanges.theirMessage: We switched to a low block second half. Just sitting deep and hitting them on the counter.

replies.text: Did it work? Were they getting through down the wings?
replies.theirResponse: Exactly. They had the ball but no end product. We got one on the break.
replies.coachNote: Asks about the effectiveness and spots the detail of the wings.

replies.text: That's smart.
replies.coachNote: Safe but doesn't engage with what she's noticing.

replies.text: Low blocks are boring to watch.
replies.theirResponse: It's not about entertainment, it's about points.
replies.coachNote: Dismissing her strategy can feel like dismissing her team.

payload.closingNote: She spotted a tactical shift; ask how it changed the match, not whether you like it.

statement.speaker: Simone
statement.text: They press like maniacs from the start. It's exhausting to play against.
statement.question: What is Simone saying?

options.text: The opponent team closes down players quickly to win the ball back
The opponent uses news outlets to intimidate teams
The opponent's high aggression is tiring for the other team to face
The opponent makes the referee blow the whistle more often

statement.translation: Pressing is closing down opponents quickly to force errors or win the ball early. A high press from the start is physically and mentally exhausting to play against.

followUps.line: Does your team press or sit back?
followUps.why: Helps her compare her team's style to what she's describing.

followUps.line: How did your midfield cope with the pressure?
followUps.why: Asks her to spot which players felt the press most.

statement.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure about the pressing intensity, ask 'How much of the pitch are they covering?' instead of guessing how hard they press.

payload.prompt: A coach says 'We counter-press.' What does she mean?

options.text: Press the opponent as soon as you lose the ball

text.text: Press the opponent only in certain zones
Defend deep and hit on the break
Press the opponent's goalkeeper

explanation.correct: Exactly. Counter-pressing means attacking immediately when you lose the ball, before the opponent is organised.
explanation.incorrect: Counter-pressing is the opposite of waiting; it's pressing immediately after losing the ball to regain it quickly.
explanation.sayThisLine: Counter-press, they won it back in four seconds.

payload.prompt: Match the defensive concept to its description.

pairs.definition: Closing down opponents quickly to win the ball or force a bad pass.
Defending deep with narrow lines to protect the box and counter quickly.
Pressing immediately after losing the ball to regain possession before the opponent organises.

explanation.summary: Pressing is about intensity; low block is about position; counter-press is about timing after a turnover.
explanation.sayThisLine: There's high press, low block and everything in between.

payload.prompt: A fan says 'We sat in a low block.' What's a good follow-up question?

options.text: Who scored?

text.text: Did they have much of the ball?
Why are low blocks boring?
Do you like that style?

explanation.correct: Good choices. Both ask her to explain what actually happened or how she felt about it.
explanation.incorrect: Jumping to the scorer or criticising the style misses the point; she's describing a tactical decision.
explanation.sayThisLine: Did it work? Did they break you down?

payload.title: Talking transfers
payload.objective: You can react to transfer news and rumours.

payload.title: Transfer speculation
payload.setting: She's nervous about a star player potentially leaving.

exchanges.theirMessage: Romano just tweeted 'here we go' with his emoji. I can't believe it's really happening.

replies.text: When did it start, the speculation or the 'here we go'?
replies.theirResponse: It's been rumoured for weeks, but the tweet means it's basically done.
replies.coachNote: Helps her separate rumour from confirmation.

replies.text: That tweet is usually legit.
replies.coachNote: Acknowledges but doesn't open the conversation.

replies.text: He was overrated anyway.
replies.coachNote: Never dunk on her favourite when she's hurting.

payload.closingNote: She's processing a player she loves leaving; acknowledge what 'here we go' means without making it worse.

statement.speaker: Mara
statement.text: He's out on loan with an option to buy. Could be permanent next summer.
statement.question: What is she explaining?

options.text: A player is borrowed for a season with a clause to buy permanently later
A player is being sold and can come back if he wants
A club can keep a player if they pay an additional fee at the end of the loan
A player is on holiday and may decide to stay

statement.translation: A loan means the player is borrowed temporarily, usually for a season. An option to buy lets the borrowing club purchase him permanently if they choose, by paying a fee.

followUps.line: Why would a club loan a player instead of selling?
followUps.why: Helps her think about financial and strategic reasons.

followUps.line: Is the option good for the player or the club that lends him?
followUps.why: Tests understanding of risk and planning.

statement.noFakeExpertNote: Transfer structures are complex; saying 'Tell me more about the deal' is smarter than guessing the terms.

payload.prompt: When a reporter tweets 'here we go,' what does it usually mean?

options.text: A transfer is rumoured but not confirmed

text.text: A transfer deal is basically done and will be announced soon
A player is leaving at the end of the season
A club is looking for a player in that position

explanation.correct: Right. 'Here we go' (especially from a reliable reporter like Romano) signals the deal is near completion.
explanation.incorrect: 'Here we go' is a report that a transfer is imminent and essentially done; vague rumours come before that.
explanation.sayThisLine: Once 'here we go' is tweeted, it's basically done.

payload.prompt: A friend tells you a star player is moving, but you haven't seen an official club announcement. How do you respond?

options.text: Ask if it's a rumour or if 'here we go' was tweeted
Assume it's official and tell others
Wait for the official club statement before reacting
Dismiss it without asking more

explanation.best: Perfect. Distinguishing between reporting tiers helps you and your friend stay informed.
explanation.acceptable: Good instinct to wait for official word, but asking for details lets you share what you know.
explanation.poor: Spreading unconfirmed news can spread misinformation, but ignoring it also leaves you out of the conversation.

payload.coachNote: Transfer news moves fast; asking 'Is it confirmed?' or 'Did Romano tweet?' shows you're engaged and careful.

payload.prompt: When a friend reacts emotionally to transfer news, what should you do?

options.text: Remind her the club knows best

text.text: Ask her what she feels she'll miss about the player
Suggest a replacement player immediately
Tell her that loans always mean players come back

explanation.correct: Good call. Letting her talk through her feelings shows you care.
explanation.incorrect: Dismissing her emotions or rushing to solutions misses the moment; listening is what matters.
explanation.sayThisLine: What will you miss about him at the club?

payload.title: Rivalry and banter
payload.objective: You can tease without being mean.

payload.title: Pre-derby trash talk
payload.setting: A friend teases you about the upcoming derby between your team and hers.

exchanges.theirMessage: Derby day incoming. Can't wait to see your team implode on the big stage.

replies.text: Cute. We'll see who's left in the table when it's over. Looking forward to it.
replies.theirResponse: Deal. First beers are on the loser.
replies.coachNote: Banter with respect and a callback to the friendship.

replies.text: That's not funny.
replies.coachNote: Banter is part of the rivalry; this reads as taking it too hard.

replies.text: Your team is trash, you're a terrible fan.
replies.coachNote: Banter is friendly; insults are not.

payload.closingNote: Derby banter is tradition; the key is laughing together afterward, not scoring points.

statement.speaker: Kai
statement.text: It's a derby, throw the form book out. Anything can happen.
statement.question: What is Kai saying?

options.text: Derby matches between local rivals ignore normal patterns and statistics
One team will win based on recent form
The underdog cannot win in a derby
Derbies are unpredictable and emotion-driven

statement.translation: A derby is a match between local rivals where emotion, history and intensity matter as much as form; the better team on paper often doesn't win.

followUps.line: What's your team's record in derbies recently?
followUps.why: Invites her to share what she knows about the rivalry.

followUps.line: Which derby has your family talked about for years?
followUps.why: Opens a door to personal history and memory.

statement.noFakeExpertNote: If you don't know the history between two rivals, ask 'What happened in the last derby?' instead of pretending.

payload.prompt: What makes banter different from insults?

options.text: Banter is mean-spirited and insults are friendly

text.text: Banter is joking with a wink; both sides can laugh after
Insults are about disagreeing; banter is about the team
Banter attacks a person's intelligence

explanation.correct: Exactly. Banter is teasing that ends with both of you laughing and still friends.
explanation.incorrect: Banter is affectionate teasing about teams; insults cross the line to hurting the person.
explanation.sayThisLine: Good banter is fun for both sides.

payload.prompt: Match the rivalry concept to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A match between local rivals with extra emotion, history and tradition.
Friendly, teasing trash talk where both sides laugh together.
A sustained competitive relationship between teams or fans that carries historical weight.

explanation.summary: Derbies are matches; banter is the conversation; rivalry is the relationship that lasts years.
explanation.sayThisLine: The derby is where banter meets rivalry.

payload.prompt: After a derby loss to a rival, how do you handle banter from their fans?

options.text: Ignore them completely

text.text: Tell them they're terrible fans
Laugh it off and promise revenge in the return fixture
Argue about why you deserved to win

explanation.correct: Perfect. This shows you can handle the loss with grace and look forward to the next match.
explanation.incorrect: Getting angry or defensive turns banter into a real argument; rising above it is the way.
explanation.sayThisLine: Fair play, we'll get you back in April.

payload.title: Match-day fan slang
payload.objective: You can decode nutmegs, rabonas and worldies.

statement.speaker: Zara
statement.text: He nutmegged the full-back and cut it back for an easy tap-in.
statement.question: What did he do?

options.text: Passed the ball between a defender's legs
Kicked the ball with his heel
Broke through the defence with a dribble
Used a rabona kick to deliver

statement.translation: To nutmeg someone is to pass the ball between their legs, leaving them behind. It's a silky skill that shows confidence.

followUps.line: Is it something you see every game?
followUps.why: Tests whether she knows how rare and special the skill is.

followUps.line: Does he do that a lot?
followUps.why: Invites her to share if it's part of his game.

statement.noFakeExpertNote: If you don't recognise the skill, ask 'What does that even look like?' instead of nodding along.

payload.title: Celebrating the messy win
payload.setting: She texts during a match where her team wins ugly.

exchanges.theirMessage: We were awful but we got the three points. That's what matters when you're fighting for the title.

replies.text: Ugly wins are champion wins. How did you scrape it?
replies.theirResponse: Second-half scramble, bit of luck, but we took our chance.
replies.coachNote: Validates her point and asks the story of the goal.

replies.text: You looked terrible.
replies.coachNote: Even if true, this reads as dismissive.

replies.text: That's not a real win.
replies.coachNote: Never diminish a win to a fan.

payload.closingNote: She's celebrating a hard-fought win; acknowledge that scrappy wins are part of the title race.

payload.prompt: A fan says a goal was 'worldie material.' What does she mean?

options.text: It was good enough to win an international award

text.text: It was spectacular enough to be remembered for years
It was the most beautiful goal ever scored
All of the above, basically

explanation.correct: Yes. A worldie is a stunning goal that sticks in your memory.
explanation.incorrect: A worldie is fan slang for an unforgettable, beautiful goal; it's subjective but the emotion is universal.
explanation.sayThisLine: That's the kind of goal you rewatch for years.

payload.prompt: Match the fan slang to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Passing the ball between an opponent's legs, leaving them behind.
A kick where the kicking foot crosses behind the standing leg.
A victory without dominance, often messy but gutsy.

explanation.summary: Skills (nutmeg, rabona) and results (scrappy win) both belong in fan conversations about what made a match memorable.
explanation.sayThisLine: That match had a nutmeg, a rabona and still felt like a scrappy win.

payload.prompt: When a friend celebrates a 'scrappy win,' what are you hearing?

options.text: She's apologising for how her team played

text.text: She's proud her team won despite playing poorly
She thinks the win doesn't count
She respects the team's mentality in grinding it out

explanation.correct: Right. A scrappy win is a point of pride; it shows character and fighting spirit.
explanation.incorrect: Scrappy isn't an apology; it's admiration for winning when things don't go to plan.
explanation.sayThisLine: That's a scrappy win, but champions need those.

payload.title: Asking a real question
payload.objective: You can ask a curious question instead of faking it.

payload.title: Genuine curiosity after a rival's win
payload.setting: Her rival's team wins and she texts to congratulate them.

exchanges.theirMessage: Fair play, your guy's performance today was unreal.

replies.text: Thanks. What was it specifically that stood out to you about him?
replies.theirResponse: His pressing in the first half. He didn't let us build.
replies.coachNote: You asked a real question and learned something new about your rival's player.

replies.text: I know.
replies.coachNote: Accepting the compliment, but missing a moment to bond.

replies.text: Your team was lucky to lose.
replies.coachNote: Never dunk on someone being gracious.

payload.closingNote: When a rival compliments your team, asking a genuine follow-up shows respect and builds the conversation.

statement.speaker: Chris
statement.text: It came down to the substitution at the hour mark. That changed everything.
statement.question: What is Chris talking about?

options.text: A tactical change the manager made that shifted the match
A player's individual skill change mid-match
The referee's decision at the hour mark
The manager's decision to replace a player altered the outcome

statement.translation: Chris is highlighting a specific manager decision (bringing on a fresh player, changing shape, or switching someone off) that swung the momentum of the match.

followUps.why: Invites you to learn the specific player and their impact.
Asks whether the move was expected or clever.

statement.noFakeExpertNote: If you didn't watch the match, saying 'Tell me who he brought on and what changed' is honest and shows real interest.

payload.prompt: After a match, what's the best question to ask a fan?

options.text: Who won?

text.text: What was the deciding moment?
Did your team play well?
Who made a mistake?

explanation.correct: Perfect. This invites her to tell the story she's thinking about.
explanation.incorrect: Asking who won or if they played well leaves little room for real conversation; asking about the key moment opens it up.
explanation.sayThisLine: What was the moment that decided it?

payload.prompt: Match the conversation skill to its benefit.

pairs.definition: Acknowledging great performance in opponents or their fans keeps friendships strong.
Asking 'What did you see?' instead of stating opinions shows genuine interest.
Discussing specific moments, players and decisions makes conversations deeper and more real.

explanation.summary: Good conversation comes from respecting others, asking real questions and talking about specifics.
explanation.sayThisLine: The best football talk comes from genuine curiosity.

payload.prompt: When should you acknowledge that a rival's player had a great game?

options.text: Only if your team wins

text.text: Never, because it's your rival
Always, when you actually saw something good
Only after a few weeks have passed

explanation.correct: Yes. Acknowledging greatness in the moment is a sign of genuine fandom and respect.
explanation.incorrect: Respect for the sport means respecting when someone plays well, regardless of the result or rivalry.
explanation.sayThisLine: That was a worldie from him, respect.
